🌱 Basics · Lesson 5 · 2 min read

AI in Everyday Life

The hidden AI you use every day — probably without noticing.

AI in your pocket

Your smartphone is packed with AI: face unlock, the keyboard that predicts your next word, voice assistants like Siri, Gemini or Alexa, and a camera that blurs the background or brightens night photos automatically. Many of these run right on your phone, without even needing the Internet.

Did you know? Many phones have a special chip just for AI, often called a neural processing unit (NPU). It runs AI tasks quickly without draining the battery.

What you watch and hear

YouTube, TikTok, Netflix and Spotify all use recommendation systems. They learn from what you watch, like, skip and replay, and compare you with millions of other users to guess what you'll enjoy next. That's why your feed feels made just for you — because, in a way, it is.

AI around the world

Maps predict traffic and find the fastest route. Banks use AI to spot unusual payments that might be fraud. Doctors use AI tools to help find signs of disease in X-rays and scans. Translators help people talk across languages, and some cars can stay in their lane and brake automatically. Scientists even used AI (AlphaFold) to predict the 3D shapes of proteins — work that won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024.

The other side of the feed

Recommendation systems are designed to keep you watching for as long as possible. They can also create a filter bubble, where you mostly see things that match what you already like or believe. Knowing that an algorithm chooses your feed puts you back in control: search for new topics, follow different voices, and take breaks when scrolling stops being fun.

Key points

  • You already use AI daily: face unlock, predictive text, maps, recommendations, spam filters.
  • Recommendation systems learn from your behaviour to keep you interested.
  • Knowing how feeds work helps you escape filter bubbles and stay in control.

Check yourself

Why does your video feed seem to know what you like?

Show the answer

Right answer: A recommendation system learns from what you watch, like and skip

Recommendation systems find patterns in your behaviour and in the behaviour of similar users, then predict what will keep you watching.
